lesson.title: Balancing the Books: Conservation of Charge
lesson.summary: In a redox equation, the total electric charge on the reactant side must equal the total electric charge on the product side, and electron transfer is the exact mechanism that guarantees it.
lesson.body:
Conservation of charge is another specific case of the general conservation laws you have studied, applied here to electric charge instead of mass. It states that the net charge on the reactant side of a balanced equation must equal the net charge on the product side. Unlike conservation of mass, the totals do not need to be zero, reacting ions can carry real net charge, they only need to match each other on both sides of the arrow.

Redox reactions are the clearest place to see this law at work, precisely because electron transfer is the mechanism that enforces it. Every electron carries a charge of exactly -1, and in a properly balanced redox equation, the number of electrons released in the oxidation half reaction is forced to equal the number absorbed in the reduction half reaction, which you saw in the electron transfer chapter. That exact match is what allows the electrons to cancel completely when the two half reactions are added together. If the electron counts did not match, the electrons would not cancel, and the combined equation would carry leftover charge that could never balance.

Verify this on the zinc and copper reaction: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) is right arrow Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s). Left side charge: neutral zinc contributes 0, and Cu2+ contributes +2, for a total of +2. Right side charge: Zn2+ contributes +2, and neutral copper metal contributes 0, also totaling +2. The charges match, +2 equals +2, even though neither side is neutral overall. That is conservation of charge in its simplest form.

Check it again on the more complex permanganate and iron equation from earlier: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ is right arrow Mn2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe3+. Left side charge: -1 from MnO4-, plus 8(+1) = +8 from the hydrogen ions, plus 5(+2) = +10 from the iron(II) ions, totaling -1 + 8 + 10 = +17. Right side charge: +2 from Mn2+, plus 0 from the neutral water molecules, plus 5(+3) = +15 from the iron(III) ions, totaling 2 + 15 = +17. Both sides carry a net charge of +17. The charges are far from zero, but they are equal, which is exactly what the law requires, and exactly what guarantees that this equation, and every properly balanced redox equation, is truly complete.
